name: Unstructured
purpose: Open-source ETL library that partitions documents of many formats into structured elements (titles, narrative text, tables, list items) with connectors for storage systems and destinations.
journalism_use_case: Building a repeatable ingest pipeline over a mixed document set with element-level structure rather than flat text: knowing that a block is a table or a heading lets downstream search and extraction behave sensibly, which matters when the corpus is thousands of filings.
pros: Element-level partitioning (title, narrative, table, list) is more useful than flat text for search ranking and for targeted extraction, and few open libraries provide it across formats
Large connector ecosystem for sources and destinations, so ingest-to-index is configuration rather than code
Apache-2.0 with very active development (0.27.37, 2026-11-06; pushed 2026-11-17) and a substantial community (15,755 stars)
Scales to batch operation and is designed for pipelines rather than interactive use, which suits corpus work
cons: Commercial-product gravity: the open library is the free tier of a commercial platform, and the most convenient paths (hosted API, managed connectors) are paid — so check what you are depending on and whether a feature might move
456 open issues and rapid version churn (a 0.27.x line), so pinning is essential and upgrades need regression testing on your own documents
Heavyweight dependency surface, with optional model-based partitioning that pulls in substantial extras
Partition quality on complex PDFs is below Docling and Marker, so it is an ingest framework rather than a best-in-class parser
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 15,755 stars with 456 open issues, release 0.27.37 (2026-11-06), pushed 2026-11-17, Apache-2.0. The commercial-platform relationship is documented by the vendor; the open library is genuinely usable standalone.
assessment: Consider it where you want an off-the-shelf ingest framework with connectors and can accept vendor-adjacent dependencies; prefer Docling plus your own orchestration where parsing fidelity and independence matter more. For your profile the risk to weigh is strategic rather than technical: building your core ingest on the free tier of a commercial product means your pipeline's future depends on that company's open-source commitment. Docling's LF AI & Data governance is a more durable foundation.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 0.27.37 (2026-11-06), 15,755 stars, 456 open issues. Same-day commits and frequent releases under commercial maintenance.
model_or_data_licence: Optional model-based partitioning uses models with their own licences — verify what you enable.
licence_restrictions: Library is permissive. The hosted API and some connectors are commercial products under separate terms.
costs: Library free. Hosted API and enterprise features are priced separately (not verified in this survey). Self-hosted costs are CPU, or GPU if model-based partitioning is enabled. Estimate.
privacy: Local when self-hosted with local partitioning. Using the hosted API sends documents to the vendor — inappropriate for source material, and the easy path, so set the configuration deliberately.
alternatives: Docling for layout-aware parsing under neutral governance
Apache Tika plus your own orchestration for maximum format coverage
MarkItDown for quick triage without pipeline ambitions

name: MinerU
purpose: Document-extraction pipeline that converts PDFs and Office documents into Markdown and JSON with layout detection, reading-order reconstruction, formula and table recognition.
journalism_use_case: High-quality conversion of technical and academic-style documents — scientific reports, engineering filings, financial statements with formulae — where layout and formula recognition matter and generic extractors produce unusable output.
pros: Formula recognition is a genuine differentiator for technical documents, which appear in environmental, medical and engineering investigations and defeat most extractors
Strong performance on Chinese-language documents, reflecting its origins — relevant if your work covers Chinese corporate or state material
Very large adoption (83,798 stars) with frequent releases (mineru-4.2.3, 2026-11-16) and an almost empty issue tracker (9 open)
Produces both Markdown and structured JSON, so it serves reading and programmatic use
cons: LICENCE CAUTION: GitHub reports NOASSERTION and session 1's licence inspection recorded 'Apache-2.0 plus additional terms (restrictive)' — so the licence is not plain Apache-2.0 and the additional terms must be read before commercial use or redistribution. This is exactly the pattern that catches newsrooms out
GPU effectively required for the full pipeline, so it is server-side infrastructure rather than a laptop tool
Model weights are distributed separately and their terms were not verified in this survey
Documentation is strongest in Chinese, and the English materials lag — a real friction for a non-Chinese-speaking team
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 83,798 stars with 9 open issues, release mineru-4.2.3 (2026-11-16), pushed 2026-11-16, SPDX NOASSERTION. Session 1's a1disc/notes.md independently recorded 'MinerU Apache-2.0+additional terms (restrictive)' after reading the licence text — a finding this entry carries forward and flags as requiring legal review.
assessment: Technically impressive and licence-ambiguous, which for your profile means: evaluate it on technical documents where its formula and layout handling would materially help, but get the additional licence terms read before anything built on it reaches publication. Docling remains the safer default for general use. If your work involves Chinese-language corporate or state documents, MinerU's advantage there may justify the legal review.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release mineru-4.2.3 published the same day, 83,798 stars, 9 open issues, SPDX NOASSERTION. Same-day release and push with near-zero backlog at very large scale — excellent activity, with licensing as the open question.
licence: Apache-2.0 with ADDITIONAL TERMS recorded as restrictive (session 1 read the licence text; GitHub reports NOASSERTION) — read the full terms before commercial use
model_or_data_licence: Model weights distributed separately; terms NOT verified in this survey.
licence_restrictions: Material and unresolved: the additional terms layered on Apache-2.0 were recorded as restrictive and have not been characterised in detail here. Obtain a legal reading before commercial deployment or redistribution.
costs: No fee. GPU host required for the full pipeline — the dominant cost. Model weight downloads. Estimate.
privacy: Local processing after weights download; no inference-time external calls in the self-hosted path. A hosted service exists at mineru.net, which would involve sending documents to the operator.
alternatives: Docling for a clean MIT position with good layout handling
Marker/Surya where the weights threshold is acceptable
PaddleOCR for Chinese-language OCR with Apache-2.0 code
blockers: Licence is Apache-2.0 plus unread additional terms recorded as restrictive — legal review required before commercial use

name: libpff
purpose: Library and tools to read Microsoft Personal Folder File formats (PST, OST, PAB), extracting messages, attachments, folder structure and metadata including recovery of deleted items.
journalism_use_case: Leaked mailboxes arrive as PST files, and this is the tool that opens them: extract messages, folder hierarchies and attachments at scale, including items deleted but still recoverable — which in a mailbox leak is frequently where the material nobody intended to keep is found.
pros: Deleted-item recovery from PST is a distinctive investigative capability: the messages someone deleted are often the most significant, and generic mail converters do not retrieve them
Reverse-engineered format documentation published alongside the code, so the extraction is explicable and defensible if challenged
LGPL-3.0 with active maintenance (pushed 2026-11-08, tag 20261030) from a maintainer with a long forensic-tooling record
Handles the awkward older PST variants that modern tools reject, which matters because leaked mailboxes are frequently old
cons: Low-level C library with tooling that assumes forensic literacy: errors are cryptic and the output needs post-processing before reporters can use it
No releases in the GitHub sense (date-stamped tags only), so pinning means recording a tag and the documentation is wiki-based
375 stars and 16 open issues — a specialist project where you may be on your own for an unusual file
Extraction only: deduplication, threading, search and review all happen in other tools, so it is one stage of a mailbox pipeline
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 375 stars with 16 open issues, latest tag 20261030, pushed 2026-11-08, LGPL-3.0. The libyal projects are standard components in digital-forensics tooling, which is the relevant adjacent evidence.
assessment: Adopt it as the PST entry point for any mailbox leak, and plan the pipeline around it: libpff to extract, Tika or your own code to normalise, datasketch to deduplicate threads, and a search index for review. For your profile the deleted-item recovery is the detail worth knowing about and building into the process explicitly, because it will not happen by default and it is frequently where the story is.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-08, no release objects, latest tag 20261030, 375 stars, 16 open issues. Date-stamped tag releases on a regular cadence from a long-committed maintainer.
licence_restrictions: LGPL-3.0 permits linking from your own tooling provided the library remains replaceable; modifications must be shared.
costs: No fee. C build toolchain; disk for extracted messages and attachments, which can exceed the PST size. Estimate.
privacy: Entirely local. The extracted mailbox is among the most sensitive material a newsroom handles — encrypted storage and strict access control are essential.
alternatives: libratom for a Python-native approach to PST and mbox with research-oriented tooling
readpst (libpst) as an alternative extractor
Apache Tika, which can read PST via libraries but without deleted-item recovery

name: libratom
purpose: Python library and CLI for parsing and processing PST and mbox email archives, extracting messages and attachments, generating reports and running spaCy entity extraction over message bodies.
journalism_use_case: A Python-native route into a leaked mailboxes with entity extraction built in: parse the PST, generate a report of senders, recipients and date ranges, and extract named entities from message bodies — a usable first pass on a mailbox without assembling four tools.
pros: Python-native with integrated entity extraction, so a first-pass analysis of a mailbox (who, when, which names recur) is a single command rather than a pipeline project
Built for archival processing of email collections by a research project focused on exactly that problem, so the reporting output is designed for exploring a collection
MIT licensed and simple enough to read, with a clean tracker (7 open issues)
Handles both PST and mbox, covering the two formats leaked mail actually arrives in
cons: Maintenance has slowed: last push 2026-01-31 with no release objects (tag 0.7.1), ten months before this survey — a research-project cadence
Does not recover deleted items the way libpff does, so for the forensically interesting content you still need libpff
Small community (130 stars), so unusual archives may need your own debugging
Entity extraction inherits spaCy's limitations on OCR-noisy or non-English content, and mailbox text is often multilingual
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 130 stars with 7 open issues, no release objects, latest tag 0.7.1, last push 2026-01-31, MIT licence. The RATOM project's archival-email focus is documented and is the relevant context for the design.
assessment: Useful as the convenient first pass on a mailbox, with libpff behind it for depth. For your profile the pattern I would use is: libratom for the quick who-talked-to-whom-and-when report that tells you whether the mailbox matters, then libpff plus a proper pipeline if it does. The slowing maintenance is tolerable for a parsing library but means pinning and being ready to own it.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-01-31, no release objects, latest tag 0.7.1, 130 stars, 7 open issues. Ten months without activity on a research-funded project — declining rather than dormant, with no deprecation notice.
model_or_data_licence: spaCy models used for entity extraction carry their own per-pipeline terms.
costs: No fee. CPU; disk for extracted content. Estimate.
privacy: Entirely local processing of highly sensitive material; the same handling obligations as any mailbox extraction apply.
alternatives: libpff for deeper extraction including deleted items
Apache Tika for format coverage without email-specific reporting
ePADD for archival email appraisal with a review interface

name: Media Cloud API client
purpose: Python client for the Media Cloud Online News Archive and Directory, providing search over a large multi-country corpus of news content with source metadata and aggregate counts over time.
journalism_use_case: Answering how coverage of a topic developed across outlets and countries without building your own news archive: query attention over time, compare which outlets covered a claim, and identify when a narrative entered mainstream coverage — a media-analysis capability that would otherwise take months of collection.
pros: Access to an existing large, multi-country news archive removes the collection problem entirely, which is the expensive part of media analysis
Source directory with country and media-type metadata lets you frame comparisons properly rather than treating all outlets as equivalent
Apache-2.0 client with active maintenance (v5.2.0 released 2026-10-06 with same-day push) and a clean tracker
Academic provenance with published methodology, so analyses built on it are citable
cons: Dependent on Media Cloud's service, access terms and continued funding — a research-institution dependency whose continuity is outside your control and which has changed shape before
Archive coverage is uneven by country and period, so an absence of coverage in the data may reflect collection gaps rather than editorial silence; this is the central analytical trap
Access requires an API key and terms that were NOT verified in this survey — check before building on it
Small client community (89 stars), so you will read source for unusual queries
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 89 stars with 3 open issues, release v5.2.0 (2026-10-06) with same-day push, Apache-2.0. Media Cloud's use in academic media research is well established; its current access terms were not verified here.
assessment: Integrate it for media-attention analysis, treating coverage gaps as the main methodological risk — always check whether the outlets you expect are actually in the collection for the period you are analysing, and say so in the methodology note. For your profile it is the pragmatic alternative to building a news archive, which is a project you should not start unless Media Cloud's coverage genuinely fails you. Verify the access terms first.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-06, latest release v5.2.0 published the same day, 89 stars, 3 open issues. Current releases tracking an operating service; the client is small and the service is the substantive dependency.
model_or_data_licence: Media Cloud archive access terms apply and were NOT verified in this survey; the underlying news content remains the publishers' copyright.
licence_restrictions: Client permissive. Archive access terms unverified — confirm before publishing derived datasets, and note that republishing article text raises publisher copyright separately.
costs: Client free. API access terms and any tiers not verified in this survey; historically free for research use with a key. Confirm before planning.
privacy: Queries go to Media Cloud, disclosing the topics and outlets you are researching to a third party. Not a concern for most media analysis; relevant if the topic itself is sensitive.
alternatives: GDELT for a different large-scale news-event archive with its own biases
Building a targeted corpus with trafilatura plus Scrapy where coverage must be exact
Internet Archive full-text search for historical web content
blockers: Service dependency with unverified access terms; uneven archive coverage by country and period

name: gdelt-doc-api
purpose: Python client for the GDELT 2.0 Document API, providing keyword and theme search over GDELT's global news monitoring with volume time series and article lists.
journalism_use_case: Rapid global coverage checks: establish whether a claim or event was reported anywhere worldwide and when it first appeared, across many languages — useful both for narrative-tracking and for finding the earliest report of an incident you are verifying.
pros: Global, multilingual coverage with a simple query interface, which makes 'has anyone reported this anywhere' answerable in seconds
Volume time series is directly useful for narrative-propagation analysis and for finding the inflection point when a story broke
MIT licensed, tiny dependency surface, free to use with no API key for the Document API
Earliest-mention lookup is a practical verification technique that complements reverse-image search for claim provenance
cons: Dormant: last push 2025-04-22 with release 1.12.0 (2025-04-03), nineteen months before this survey — a thin client over a stable API, so the risk is low but real
GDELT's own data has well-known quirks: automated event coding and theme extraction produce noise, duplicate articles are common, and source quality is unweighted
Dependent on GDELT's free API remaining available and unchanged; a thin client offers no protection if it does not
Small community (234 stars) and 2 open issues — minimal support
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 234 stars with 2 open issues, release 1.12.0 (2025-04-03), last push 2025-04-22, MIT licence. GDELT's noise characteristics are widely documented in media-research literature rather than being a criticism of this client.
assessment: Keep it for quick global coverage checks and first-mention lookups, where it is genuinely fast and useful. For your profile the discipline is to treat GDELT output as a pointer rather than a measurement: duplicate and low-quality sources inflate volume, so never publish a GDELT count as a finding — use it to find the articles, then read them. The dormancy is acceptable for a thin client, and reimplementing it against the API would take an afternoon if it breaks.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2025-04-22, latest release 1.12.0 (2025-04-03), 234 stars, 2 open issues. Nineteen months inactive. Low practical risk because it is a thin wrapper over an external API with a stable interface.
model_or_data_licence: GDELT data terms apply to the underlying archive and were not verified in this survey; article content remains the publishers' copyright.
licence_restrictions: Client unrestricted. Check GDELT's own terms before republishing data derived from it.
costs: No fee; the GDELT Document API is free. Negligible compute.
privacy: Queries go to GDELT, disclosing your search terms to that service.
alternatives: Media Cloud for a curated archive with better source metadata
Direct GDELT BigQuery access for large-scale analysis, at Google Cloud query cost
Your own targeted corpus where precision matters more than breadth
blockers: Dormant client; GDELT data noise means counts are not publishable as findings

name: Huginn
purpose: Self-hosted system for building agents that monitor sources and act on events: fetch web pages and feeds, extract data, evaluate conditions, transform and emit to other agents or notification channels.
journalism_use_case: Newsroom automation without writing a service: build an agent chain that watches a court docket page, extracts new case numbers, cross-references them against a watchlist and posts matches to an internal channel — the kind of workflow that otherwise lives in a fragile cron script nobody maintains.
pros: Agent-and-event model handles the common monitoring pattern (watch, extract, filter, notify) declaratively, so workflows are visible and editable rather than buried in scripts
Self-hosted with a very large community (50,560 stars) and active maintenance (v2026.11.09 released 2026-11-09, same-day push)
MIT licensed, so there is no copyleft or fair-code restriction — a notable contrast with n8n in the same role
Long-lived: a decade of operation means the agent library covers most sources and sinks you would want
cons: Ruby on Rails application with a substantial operational footprint and 692 open issues — running it well is a commitment, and a neglected Huginn fails silently
The agent UI becomes unwieldy past a few dozen workflows, and there is no good versioning of agent configurations, so a complex setup is hard to review or reproduce
Debugging a broken chain is awkward: failures surface as empty events rather than clear errors, which is the same silent-failure problem as any monitoring system
Dated interface and conventions compared with modern automation platforms, which affects adoption by non-engineers
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 50,560 stars with 692 open issues, release v2026.11.09 (2026-11-09) with same-day push, MIT licence. A long-established self-hosted automation project with a very large community.
assessment: Worth adopting where newsroom automation is a recurring need and you prefer MIT-licensed infrastructure to n8n's fair-code licence — that licence difference is the main reason to choose Huginn in 2026. For your profile the practical caution is configuration management: export agent definitions into version control so your automation is reviewable and rebuildable, because the UI-only configuration is otherwise an undocumented single point of failure.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-09, latest release v2026.11.09 published the same day, 50,560 stars, 692 open issues. Date-versioned releases with current commits from a community team; the backlog reflects a decade of accumulation.
licence_restrictions: None — notably unrestricted compared with n8n's Sustainable Use Licence for the same use case.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure estimate: a Rails host plus a database and background workers — one modest VM for a small newsroom. Operating effort is moderate and ongoing. Assumptions: self-hosted, dozens of workflows.
privacy: Fully self-hosted; monitored sources and extracted data stay internal. Notification agents send data to whatever channel you configure, so sinks are the exposure point.
alternatives: n8n for a more modern interface — but note its Sustainable Use Licence is not open source
changedetection.io plus webchanges for monitoring without general automation
Scripted cron jobs in version control, which are less visible but easier to review

name: n8n
purpose: Visual workflow-automation platform with hundreds of integrations, code nodes, scheduling and native AI/agent capabilities, self-hostable or used as a hosted service.
journalism_use_case: Building newsroom automation that non-engineers can read and modify: a visual workflow that watches a source, extracts data, calls a language model for classification and posts to a channel — with the logic visible to an editor rather than hidden in a script.
pros: Integration breadth and a genuinely usable visual editor mean workflows are accessible to colleagues who would never read a script, which affects whether automation survives staff changes
Native AI and agent nodes make language-model steps a first-class part of a workflow, which is where newsroom automation is heading
Enormous community (210,772 stars) and very active development (n8n@2.48.4, 2026-11-13; pushed 2026-11-17)
Self-hostable, so data and credentials can stay on your infrastructure
cons: LICENCE BLOCKER for some uses: n8n is under the Sustainable Use Licence (fair-code), NOT an OSI open-source licence — session 1 recorded this independently and GitHub reports NOASSERTION. It restricts commercial redistribution and offering n8n as a service, which matters if you want to provide workflows to partner organisations
1,267 open issues and very rapid development, so pinning and upgrade testing are necessary
Visual workflows at scale become hard to review and diff, and credentials embedded in workflows need careful handling
Commercial-product gravity: the hosted service and enterprise features are the vendor's business, and feature availability can shift between tiers
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 210,772 stars with 1,267 open issues, release n8n@2.48.4 (2026-11-13), pushed 2026-11-17, SPDX NOASSERTION. Session 1's a1disc/notes.md independently recorded 'n8n Sustainable Use License (fair-code)' after reading the licence — a finding carried forward here, and the decisive consideration for anyone assuming it is open source.
assessment: Capable and widely adopted, and not open source — which is the fact to be clear about. For internal newsroom automation the Sustainable Use Licence is unlikely to bite, so it is usable; if you intend to host workflows for partner organisations or build a product, read the licence properly first or choose Huginn, which is MIT. For your profile I would default to Huginn on licence grounds unless n8n's AI nodes and visual editor are decisive for your team's ability to maintain the automation.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release n8n@2.48.4 (2026-11-13), 210,772 stars, 1,267 open issues, SPDX NOASSERTION. Same-day commits and frequent releases under well-funded commercial maintenance.
licence: Sustainable Use Licence (fair-code) — NOT an OSI open-source licence; GitHub reports NOASSERTION
model_or_data_licence: n/a for the platform; AI nodes use whichever model provider you configure, under that provider's terms.
licence_restrictions: Material: the Sustainable Use Licence permits internal business use but restricts commercial redistribution and hosting n8n as a service for third parties. A newsroom running it internally is fine; a newsroom offering workflow hosting to partners should read the licence and probably choose differently.
costs: Self-hosting the community edition has no licence fee under the Sustainable Use Licence. Hosted n8n Cloud and enterprise editions are priced per workflow-execution or per seat (not verified in this survey). If AI nodes call hosted models, those token costs apply. Estimate.
privacy: Self-hosting keeps workflow data and credentials internal. Two exposure points to manage: AI nodes pointed at hosted model providers send content to them, and integration credentials stored in n8n make the instance a high-value target.
alternatives: Huginn for an MIT-licensed self-hosted equivalent — recommended on licence grounds
Scripted pipelines in version control for engineer-maintained automation
Apache Airflow or Dagster where the workload is data-pipeline rather than event automation
blockers: Sustainable Use Licence (fair-code) is not open source and restricts offering n8n as a service to third parties
